structured_output.hypothesis: Among cones of one species sharing a given parastichy arrangement, the share with right-handed (versus left-handed) spirals for the stated series is statistically indistinguishable from 50%.
structured_output.pass_criterion: In a per-cone dataset of at least 200 cones of one conifer species with the same parastichy arrangement, a two-sided exact binomial test of the right-handed count against p=0.5 gives p>=0.05 and the right-handed proportion lies within 0.45-0.55 (Thompson's own figures: 224/467=0.48).
structured_output.fail_criterion: Exact binomial p<0.05 against 50:50, or a right-handed proportion outside 0.40-0.60, in such a dataset.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Direction' of the five-series is the handedness (clockwise or anticlockwise) of the parastichy family with the lower count, recorded per cone. 'Nearly equally divided' is operationalised as a binomial test not rejecting 50:50 plus a proportion within 0.45-0.55. No modern reinterpretation is needed, but the dataset must be per-cone and from one species.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: Three rounds of searching found no public per-cone parastichy handedness dataset for Norway spruce or any other extant conifer. The searches covered the web, Dryad and Zenodo, and figshare was covered only in the earlier round. The Dryad search page returned HTTP 403. The Zenodo search page showed no results for the query. The web searches found only journal papers that report handedness counts in their text: slash pine, lodgepole pine, black pine, and fossil Araucaria mirabilis cones. The Araucaria cones are fossil and so outside the claim's scope. I could not confirm that any of these papers has a data deposit, and I fetched no dataset landing page, so I name none rather than risk an unverified identifier. The claim could be tested only by new counts or by digitising the tables in the published papers.
